clue.text: One getting lift on trail, resembling the other one?

definitions.note: the other one is the other 1 in the grid, 1-down, the rainbow goddess whose name is also the coloured part of the eye; this is an adjective phrase

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I
a lift is a ride in someone's car
a scent is the trail an animal leaves for hounds to follow

explanation.surface: Someone hitches a ride along a path and somehow ends up looking like a companion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the other one' points to the other light numbered 1, 1-down, the rainbow goddess Iris; shimmering with rainbow colours is resembling her.
explanation.definitionFit: Shimmering with rainbow colours means looking like the rainbow goddess, a cross-reference definition.

clue.text: One such as Murdoch getting one in the eye

definitions.meaning: the novelist Murdoch's first name, an example of a woman bearing it
the coloured ring around the pupil is part of the eye

explanation.surface: The novelist suffers a jab in the eye.
explanation.definitionFit: Murdoch the novelist had this first name, and it is also the coloured part of the eye: two senses.

clue.text: Daily features suffer here

parts.note: the word daily contains ail (suffer) in the middle of D and Y, so the place it is found reads as a location; and the newspaper nickname is a daily

explanation.surface: A newspaper's articles take a beating in its own pages.
explanation.walkthrough: DAILY has AIL, meaning suffer, sitting between D and Y; so where 'suffer' is found is in D-Y. The whole also names a daily paper, the Independent, nicknamed the Indy.
explanation.definitionFit: The Independent, a British national newspaper, is nicknamed with this short form, and it was a daily paper.

clue.text: Being heard to dry up?

parts.note: ens is the philosophers' Latin word for being or existence
ear is hearing, the faculty by which a thing is heard, as in playing by ear

explanation.surface: Something when listened to seems to make you parched.
explanation.walkthrough: ENS is a philosophical term for an entity or being, little known outside crosswords.
explanation.definitionFit: This archaic verb means to make dry and withered, as heat sears and parches, a direct synonym.

clue.text: Orderly concerned with spores at large, examples being 1ac/9, 6/19, 13ac/21, 15/13dn, 20ac/26, 22/6, 25/8, 1dn/24 and 12/7

definitions.note: each listed pair matches up in some way, so the pairs are instances of matching links; plural like the answer

indicators.note: put in order, so the letters are arranged afresh
roaming free, so the spores' letters scatter as well

explanation.surface: A hospital orderly worries about spores loose in the ward, listing cases.
explanation.walkthrough: Each pair links: anagrams (1ac/9), rival schools (6/19), a repeat (13ac/21), a sound-alike (15/13dn), multiples (20ac/26), a letter change (22/6), opposites (25/8), eye parts (1dn/24), and two halves of an idiom (12/7).
explanation.definitionFit: Each pair listed is a match or analogy between two answers, so they are instances of matching links.

clue.text: Sewer at point of origin having progress impeded in E3?

parts.note: nee means born, giving where one started
progress impeded is held up; in Cockney East London (E3 is the Bow postcode) the H is dropped, giving 'eld, and in a down light up reads as upward

explanation.surface: A sewage drain at its source in East London gets blocked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sewer' looks like a drain but is one who sews. Progress impeded is 'held up'; E3 is Bow in Cockney London, so the H drops to 'ELD, and 'up' in a down clue runs it upwards to DLE.
explanation.definitionFit: The sewing tool that carries the thread through cloth is literally a thing that sews.

clue.text: 90-360 degrees would get you here? A little overqualified, perhaps!

definitions.note: the place a quarter-turn-plus from east to north lands you is the famous school

parts.note: on a compass bearing, 90 degrees is due east, E
the dash between two numbers is read as 'to'
a bearing of 360 degrees is due north, N

explanation.surface: A turn on the compass lands you at a posh school, which may leave you slightly overqualified.
explanation.walkthrough: The range 90-360 reads as 'E to N'. The closing exclamation is a wry aside that the famous public school turns out pupils who are, if anything, overqualified.
explanation.definitionFit: The location is the famous English public school near Windsor, the place the compass journey brings you to.

clue.text: See 12
Where working cobbler is not receiving any 25

definitions.meaning: a cobbler works beside the last, the foot-shaped block on which shoes are made
25 is precedence; second from the end is a position with no priority, an adverb phrase

explanation.surface: A busy shoemaker is not given any priority.
explanation.walkthrough: A cobbler's last is the foot-shaped form he works on, so he sits beside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Penultimate, the place before the end, gets no priority; and the cobbler sits by his foot-shaped form: two senses.

clue.text: 1ac 1ac? Tactless!

indicators.note: the second 1ac, read as its answer meaning shimmering and shifting, signals that the first one's letters shift into a new order

parts.note: the first 1ac stands for the 1-across answer, whose ten letters are the fodder; the same reference repeated then serves as the signal

explanation.surface: A bare cross-reference repeated, followed by an exclamation about a lack of tact.
explanation.walkthrough: Both 1ac references stand for the 1-across answer: the first is the fodder, the second, meaning shimmering and changeable, is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe someone who lacks discretion and blurts out what should stay private: a synonym.

clue.text: Those born in the '60s reading what follows chapter IX of book I

parts.note: Genesis is the first book of the Bible, abbreviated Gen
after chapter nine comes chapter ten, the Roman numeral X

explanation.surface: An instruction on where to read in a text, oddly defining a whole generation.
explanation.walkthrough: Answer order puts the book abbreviation first, so 'of' simply joins the two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Generation X is the label for people born from the early 1960s to around 1980.

clue.text: A couple of travelling spacemen crashing as a result of a fault?

indicators.note: a crash scatters wreckage, so these letters fall into a new order
a couple means two, so the first two letters of the word are taken

explanation.surface: Two astronauts on a journey come down to earth after a mistake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fault' looks like blame for a crash but is a geological fault, a fracture in the rock.
explanation.definitionFit: A steep slope or cliff often forms along a geological fault line where rock has shifted.

clue.text: To prepare for trouble when news is broadcast, cheers Coe doing reverse laps

indicators.note: to lap is to wrap round, so the turned name wraps around the rest
the runner's first name goes backwards

parts.note: Seb Coe, the British middle-distance runner
the BBC evening bulletin is the News at Ten
a drinking toast, 'down the hatch'

explanation.surface: A sports report on Seb Coe running laps the wrong way, cheered on as the news goes out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'laps' sounds athletic but is the container signal: BES (SEB turned round by 'doing reverse') goes around AT TEN plus DOWN THE HATCH. The answer spans 12 and 7 down.
explanation.definitionFit: Sailors fastened hatch covers with battens before a storm, so the idiom means to get ready for difficulty.

clue.text: See 21
Some say successful proof reader will range more than once

indicators.note: what some people say signals words heard rather than read

parts.note: a good proof reader will see errors

explanation.surface: People say a good proof reader will roam far and wide.
explanation.walkthrough: 'range' looks like a verb, to wander; it is a noun, a mountain range, and 'more than once' makes it plural.
explanation.definitionFit: Spanish-named mountain chains with jagged peaks; several of them are multiple ranges.

clue.text: D—– sturdy in constitution, but on the pill?

parts.note: the letter D with a dash, as an expletive is written, gives just the D
rugged means robust and tough in build

explanation.surface: A tough type with a censored name turns out to be taking pills.
explanation.walkthrough: The dashes mimic a censored swear word, leaving only its initial letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Having taken a sedating tablet means being under a drug's influence, so 'on the pill' is a playful paraphrase.

clue.text: A whiff of Sussex school teacher accepting poor, then very good grade?

indicators.note: to accept is to take in, so the teacher holds the grades within

parts.note: pupils address a male school teacher as sir
E is a poor exam grade
AA is a top-grade rating, a double A

explanation.surface: A teacher at a Sussex school reluctantly passes a weak pupil and then a strong one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sussex school teacher' looks like one phrase; 'A whiff of Sussex' is the definition. Sussex is a seaside county on England's south coast.
explanation.definitionFit: Sussex has a long coastline, so a breath of its bracing ocean breeze is a whiff of the place: definition by example.

clue.text: Wandering soldier wants to be human at the front

indicators.note: says the piece meaning being human comes before the soldier

parts.note: from the proverb 'to err is human'
a soldier ant is a worker of the warrior caste

explanation.surface: A soldier longs to be treated as a person while serving on the front line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'soldier' wants to be a military man, but it is an insect, and 'front' sounds military but only orders the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Roaming or straying from the proper path, as in a knight-errant who travels in search of adventure.

clue.text: Man's in pathetic poncho, wrestling with alligator

definitions.note: the possessive is an adjective sense: belonging to or concerning mankind

indicators.note: something pathetic is in a sorry state, so the poncho's letters are mangled
a wrestling bout tangles the two together, mixing the alligator's letters in too

explanation.surface: A man in a shabby poncho grapples with an alligator.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Man' looks like the wrestler but is mankind, the study of whom is anthropology.
explanation.definitionFit: Relating to the study of humankind, so pertaining to Man as a species.

clue.text: I love it, going after 70s music fan

indicators.note: the exclamation is placed after the music

parts.note: punk rock was the music of the late 1970s
ah is an exclamation of pleasure

explanation.surface: Someone sighs with delight at being a devotee of seventies music.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fan' looks like a devotee of the music; it is a large swinging cloth fan used in India.
explanation.definitionFit: A large cloth fan hung from the ceiling and worked by a servant pulling a cord, from colonial India.

clue.text: One ground-breaking school

definitions.meaning: a farm implement with spikes that breaks up soil after ploughing
a famous public school in north-west London

explanation.surface: A pioneering school.
explanation.definitionFit: It is both a spiked frame dragged over ploughed land and the famous London public school, two senses.

clue.text: Game's 1-1, after header from Scholes

definitions.note: reads 'Game is', the 's being a link

indicators.note: the odds come after the initial
the head of a word is its first letter, punning on a football header

parts.note: odds of one to one are called evens in betting

explanation.surface: A football match is level at one apiece after Paul Scholes scores with his head.
explanation.walkthrough: Paul Scholes was a Manchester United midfielder; the football picture hides a rugby game. Rugby sevens is the seven-a-side version of rugby union.
explanation.definitionFit: Seven-a-side rugby is a sport, so it is a game.

clue.text: Resurgent Man U missing midfield snapper

indicators.note: the middle letters of the nine are dropped, punning on the football midfield
rising again, read in a down light as coming up, so the nickname reads upwards

parts.note: Manchester United's nickname is the Red Devils

explanation.surface: A revived Manchester United play without their midfielders and lose a striker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Resurgent' turns REDDEVILS to SLIVEDDER; 'missing midfield' drops its middle VED. A slider is a freshwater turtle, and a snapper is also a turtle.
explanation.definitionFit: The red-eared slider is a turtle, and snapping turtles are called snappers: a loose turtle-for-turtle equivalence.

clue.text: Very, very tired, a model's got energised as 'Model Remodelled'

definitions.note: an adjective phrase: utterly hackneyed, worn out from repetition

indicators.note: energised suggests stirring something up, so the first group of letters is jumbled
to remodel is to reshape, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A worn-out model gets a jolt of energy when billed as the newly made-over version.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer spans this light and 13-across. Both halves are anagrams: A MODEL'S rearranged, then AS MODEL rearranged, each giving the same seven letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The doubled idiom means tediously familiar, the same thing yet again; 'tired' here is stale rather than sleepy.

clue.text: Top striker giving energy to boot

parts.note: E is the physics symbol for energy
to boot means as well, too

explanation.surface: A star footballer brings energy to his kicking.
explanation.walkthrough: Samuel Eto'o is a Cameroonian striker who played for Barcelona and Inter Milan; 'boot' looks like football gear but means 'in addition'.
explanation.definitionFit: Samuel Eto'o was among the world's leading strikers at the time: definition by example.

clue.text: Compulsive's heading off waterway

indicators.note: the head of the word, its first letter, goes off

parts.note: a canal is a man-made waterway

explanation.surface: An obsessive type sets off along a canal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heading off' sounds like setting out but drops the first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Short for anal-retentive: fussily obsessive about order and detail, a colloquial synonym.

clue.text: Hutton & co getting one in the eye

definitions.meaning: Len Hutton, the Yorkshire and England cricket captain, and others with his first name
the transparent focusing body inside the eye

explanation.surface: A cricketer and his teammates take a blow in the eye.
explanation.walkthrough: Sir Len Hutton was a famous England cricket captain of the 1950s.
explanation.definitionFit: Plural of the cricketer's first name, and the eye's focusing part: two senses.

clue.text: Just about withdraw coppers: overarching priority

indicators.note: the coins arch over, enclosing the shortened withdrawal word

parts.note: copper coins are pennies, pence

indicators.note: just about means almost, so the word stops short of its final letter

parts.note: to recede is to withdraw or pull back

explanation.surface: An officer barely manages to pull police off a case that has top priority.
explanation.walkthrough: 'coppers' suggests police but means coins; 'overarching' looks like part of the definition but is the container signal, and 'Just about' drops the last E of RECEDE.
explanation.definitionFit: Having the right to come first is having precedence, a direct synonym of priority.

clue.text: What helps to make sex-kitten snuggly? XXX

definitions.note: three Roman Xs, each worth ten

indicators.note: the letters that help make up the phrase are a run within it

explanation.surface: A racy question about what makes a sexy woman cuddly, answered with three kisses or an X-rated label.
explanation.walkthrough: XXX looks like kisses or an adult rating, but read as Roman numerals it is three of the number.
explanation.definitionFit: Each Roman numeral X is worth ten, so three of them written together are a plural of that number.

clue.text: Drunken Ross greedily eats round sponges

indicators.note: the greedy eating goes around the rearranged name

parts.note: to swill is to gulp down greedily

indicators.note: a drunken person staggers, so the name's letters reel into a new order

explanation.surface: A tipsy man named Ross gobbles bread rolls.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rolls' is hidden in the answer; 'round' looks like the shape of the rolls but places the letters inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Rolled sponge cakes filled with jam are sponges in the cake sense, so this is a plural example.
